newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban open new Afghan front, attack Dostum.
newsitem.headline: Taleban open new Afghan front, attack Dostum.

text.p: Taleban militia said on Friday they had captured one of six provinces held by a northern leader in their first reported offensive against his forces, snuffing out hopes of a ceasefire among Afghanistan's warring factions.

The report followed the first public attacks by Taleban leaders in Kabul on Abdul Rashid Dostum, the Uzbek leader who has allied his forces with those of former goverment military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted the Taleban governor in Herat province, Mullah Yar Mohammad, as saying his forces took control of the northwestern province of Badghis after heavy fighting against Dostum soldiers.
Yar Mohammad said Dostum had about 2,000 troops in Badghis, of whom the Taleban captured 110, including a general identified only as Hayatullah.
Later Taleban forces advanced into adjoining Dostum-held Faryab province and captured the southwestern district of Quaysar on Friday night, the AIP said.
There was no immediate confirmation of the report. The two provinces border Turkmenistan, which like other former Soviet Central Asian states have viewed events in Afghanistan with growing alarm.
It was the first report by the Taleban that its forces were directly attacking those of Dostum, a former communist military chief who the Taleban have been careful not to antagonise.
At Friday prayers in the capital a Taleban preacher told worshippers Dostum was "a former communist and a criminal", signalling the purist movement was renewing verbal attacks on the general.
The Taleban, which took the capital four weeks ago vowing to impose a pure Islamic state, appear to have abandoned their stance of calling him a man they could do business with.

Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said on Thursday Dostum had committed his forces to fighting north of Kabul, the first such acknowledgement his troops were fighting alongside those of Masood.
On Friday, the mullah preaching at Kabul's Blue Mosque reverted to the language the Taleban had used against Dostum before taking the capital four weeks ago.
The mullah also called Masood a "Dostum commander", suggesting the Uzbek leader was now regarded as the main enemy.
The mullah's bodyguards declined to name him.
The Taleban's attack, which the AIP said began on Thursday night, appears to dash lingering hopes for a ceasefire in the latest round of Afghanistan's long-running civil war.
U.N. mediator Norbert Holl and Pakistan have both said they are leading separate efforts to broker a ceasefire but there was no immediate word on Friday of any progress.
Until Friday's report of fighting in the northwest, Masood and Taleban forces have clashed mainly on the plains north of Kabul.
Masood, backed by Dostum fighters, has tried to fight his way to Kabul but faced stiff resistance on the capital's two northern roads some 30 minutes' drive from Kabul.
Two Taleban jets flew repeated sorties over the battlefield on Friday as artillery fired at the village of Kalakan where at least 14 civilians were killed by a Taleban bomber on Thursday.

But the front line itself has changed little over the past week despite efforts by Masood forces to dislodge the Taleban from a strategic pass on the eastern road out of the city. By dusk the road was quiet, with many Taleban bending in prayer.
Masood commanders have been operating out of Kalakan, 25 km (15 miles) north of Kabul, as their forces tried to break through Taleban lines over the past few days.
Taleban fighters near the front line said they tried again on Thursday night, but were repulsed. There was no independent confirmation of the report.
Reuter correspondent Chris Bird reported from the northern side of the front lines that one jet fighter tried to bomb the town of Jabal os-Siraj, some 90 km (55 miles) north of Kabul.
The bomb landed in a field and no one was hurt. There were no immediate reports of what the targets of the other raids were.
